summary: This program stores three Book objects in a list, then walks through that list and copies every book whose genre is "Fantasy" into a second list, which it prints. It is the standard pattern for filtering a collection: loop, test, collect.

lines.text: ArrayList is the concrete, resizable list class you will use most often; it has to be imported because it lives in the java.util package.
List is the interface that ArrayList implements, and importing it lets you declare variables by the general type rather than the specific class.

The variable's type is the List interface while the object created is an ArrayList, a habit that keeps the rest of the code from depending on which list implementation you chose. The <Book> tells the compiler this list holds only Book objects.

lines.code: Book sherlock = new Book("The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes", "Arthur Conan Doyle", "Mystery");
lines.text: Each book is built first and given its own variable, so the three arguments matching title, author, and genre stay readable.
add appends an object to the end of the list; the list grows on its own, unlike an array with a fixed length.
A second, empty list acts as the destination for the matches. Filtering never modifies the original collection; it builds a new one.
The enhanced for loop hands you each element of books in turn as the variable book, which is cleaner than managing an index yourself.

equalsIgnoreCase compares the text of two strings while treating upper and lower case as the same, so "fantasy" and "FANTASY" both match. Never use == to compare strings in Java, because that asks whether they are the same object rather than the same characters.
A matching book is added to the results list, so both lists now refer to the very same Book object rather than a copy.
A separate loop over the filtered list keeps the two jobs, selecting and reporting, clearly apart.
Printing an object calls its toString method automatically, which is why Book defines one that produces readable output instead of a memory address.
